newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu studies peace plan, capital jittery.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu studies peace plan, capital jittery.

text.p: Zaire's veteran president, Mobutu Sese Seko, is studying a South African peace plan after returning to his jittery capital where many people fear a battle is inevitable.

South Africa's Nelson Mandela, who is trying to avert bloodshed in the city of five million people, told a news conference in Cape Town after talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila that Mobutu had promised to respond by Monday.

Kabila, whose forces control three quarters of the huge Central African nation, said the rebels would wait for Mobutu's response, but, asked if he would halt the rebel advance on Kinshasa, he replied: "I have nothing to say about it."
Kinshasa was very quiet as it began its third night of curfew of the seven-month-old conflict.
Shops were shuttered, businesses closed early. The normally bustling streets emptied ominously well before sundown.

Earlier, state television showed Mobutu, who has cancer, descending the steps of his plane on the arm of his wife Bobi Ladawa one day after Mandela's efforts to stage peace talks on a South African ship in Congo collapsed.
An airline office in a downtown hotel said that the airport was effectively closed. The last commercial flight -- South African Airways -- left on Wednesday.
Witnesses said the road to the airport, 25 km (16 miles) from the centre of the city, was eery and largely deserted. Tense and aggressive members of the security forces patrolled.
One unconfirmed report, in a city where rumours circulated wildly, said the airport had been fired on.
A later report, endorsed by diplomats, said Mobutu's presidential guard intervened to curb looting by other soldiers about 15 km (10 miles) beyond the airport.
Residents in Kinshasa fear a rampage by Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined army as much as anything else.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries since seizing power in 1965, reputedly ammassing a huge fortune on the way.

He agreed at peace talks on May 4 to hand power to an elected president. Kabila, then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Mandela has tabled a two-page proposal for a transition to democracy in Zaire. "We are confident we are making progress," he said after talks with Kabila. "Matters are going to plan."
The South African Broadcasting Corporation, quoting a leaked copy of the proposal, said it would require Mobutu to step down within 24 hours of signing a settlement.
Rebel justice "commissioner-general" Mwenze Kongolo, quoted by Portugal's Lusa news agency on Thursday, said Mobutu ran the risk of capture if he remained in power until Saturday.
The government says the front line is some 200 km (120 miles) east of Kinshasa. The rebels say they are much closer.
"We're heading directly for a bloodbath," Mobutu aide Kabuya Lumuna said on Thursday. "Kabila knows he has the upper hand."
Mobutu opponent Mukendi wa Mulumba said confrontation was inevitable. "We will have two or three bad days from now on."
Across the river in Brazzaville, U.S., British, French, Belgian and Portuguese troops waited to pluck foreign nationals to safety should a battle for Kinshasa begin.
